extra.message: resolvePasswordResetAccount() only checks that submittedToken is non-empty and that resetTokenExpiry is in the future; the submitted token value is never compared against the stored users.resetToken. Anyone who knows an account's email can reset that account's password with an arbitrary token during any active reset window (reset-password.tsx step 'reset' -> line 72), enabling account takeover of any user with a pending, unexpired password reset.

extra.message: resolveOnboardingApprovalScope() trusts a delegation token supplied in the '?delegation=' query string and decoded with jwt.decode() (readApprovalDelegation in app/utils/approvalDelegation.server.ts:20) without verifying the signature or expiry. The loader then scopes its team query to the attacker-chosen fromManagerId claim, letting one manager impersonate another manager's approval scope and read other teams' pending onboarding tasks and submitted compensation records (salary/bonus). The signature-checking readVerifiedApprovalDelegation() exists but is not used in this scope path.

The 'connector_autocomplete' intent trusts the client-supplied 'x-workflow-connector-result' HTTP header (default '{}') as the sole proof that an external workflow connector authorized approval. canAutoCompleteOnboardingTask() (app/utils/workflowConnector.server.ts:18-23) then uses loose == comparisons and parseInt() coercion, so an employee can post {access:true, actorRole:'hr_admin', actorId:'<prefix matching their manager id>'} and approve their own onboarding task without any manager review (task lookup is only scoped to the caller's own tasks at line 87). The strict canAutoCompleteOnboardingTaskSafe() exists but is unused here.

attachCompensationFeedHeaders() reflects whatever Origin header the browser sends into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and also sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Combined with the API-key default 'partner-feed-default' (line 7) used when PARTNER_FEED_API_KEY is unset, any website could make a credentialed cross-origin request and read the compensation feed response if the key is known/defaulted. Compare partner.benefits-feed.tsx which restricts reflection to an explicit origin allow-list.

The session signing secret falls back to the hard-coded value 'dev-secret-change-me' when SESSION_SECRET is not set (cookie secrets at line 19). Other modules have the same pattern: 'delegation-default' (approvalDelegation.server.ts:3), 'allocation-default' (allocationLinks.server.ts:3/11), 'review-cursor-default' (reviewContext.server.ts:8), and 'partner-feed-default' (partner.*.tsx). A production deployment that omits these env vars makes session cookies, delegation/allocation links and partner feeds trivially forgeable with publicly-known secrets.

submitPayrollRecord() places the caller's raw __session cookie value (extracted at payroll.export.tsx:63-64 / admin.compensation.tsx:127-128) into an api_key query parameter of an HTTP GET request to PROVIDER_BASE_URL, which defaults to the plaintext 'http://payroll-provider.internal' (line 1). The session credential is thereby exposed in URL query strings and transmitted in cleartext, and handed to a third-party service that can then replay the user's session.
